paragraphs: Ivan had now gone to see Smerdyakov for the third time since coming back from Moscow. The first time was the day he arrived, when he saw him and talked with him. He went once more two weeks later, and then his visits stopped. By now more than a month had passed since he last saw him, and in that time he had heard next to nothing about him.

Ivan did not get back until five days after his father’s death, so he missed the funeral, which was held the day before he arrived. The delay was caused by Alyosha not knowing his Moscow address. He had to ask Katerina Ivanovna to telegraph Ivan, and she did not know it either, so she wired her sister and aunt, expecting Ivan to call on them the moment he reached Moscow. He did not go to them until four days after he arrived. When the telegram finally reached him, he naturally rushed to our town. Alyosha met him first. Ivan was very surprised to find that Alyosha, against the opinion of the whole town, would not suspect Mitya and spoke openly of Smerdyakov as the murderer. Later, after he had seen the police captain and the prosecutor and heard the details of the charge and the arrest, Alyosha surprised him still more. Ivan could explain his view only as exaggerated brotherly feeling and sympathy for Mitya, of whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, was very fond.

Now, since we are on the subject, a word or two about how Ivan felt toward his brother Dmitri. He simply disliked him. At most he sometimes pitied him, and even that pity was mixed with strong contempt, almost disgust. Everything about Mitya, even his looks, put him off. Ivan watched Katerina Ivanovna’s love for his brother with indignation. Still, he went to see Mitya on the very day he arrived, and the visit, far from shaking his belief in Mitya’s guilt, made it stronger. He found his brother agitated and keyed up. Mitya talked a lot, but he was very absent-minded and could not keep to the point. His language was violent, he accused Smerdyakov, and he was terribly confused. Mostly he talked about the three thousand roubles, which he said his father had “stolen” from him.
“It was my money, mine,” Mitya kept saying. “Even if I’d stolen it, I’d have had a right to.”

He barely argued with the evidence against him, and when he did try to twist some fact in his favor, he did it absurdly and without any logic. He hardly seemed to care about defending himself, whether to Ivan or to anyone. On the contrary, he was angry and scornful, proud in his contempt for the charges, and kept flying into rages and abusing everybody. Grigory’s testimony about the open door only made him laugh with contempt, and he said that “the devil opened it.” But he could give no sensible explanation of the fact. He even managed to insult Ivan at that first meeting. He told him sharply that men who preached that “everything is lawful” had no business suspecting and cross-examining him. In short, he was anything but friendly to Ivan that day. Immediately after seeing Mitya, Ivan went to see Smerdyakov for the first time.

All the way from Moscow on the train he had kept thinking about Smerdyakov and about their last conversation, the evening before he left. Much of it struck him as puzzling and suspicious. Yet when he gave his statement to the investigating lawyer, he said nothing about that conversation, for the moment. He held it back until he had seen Smerdyakov, who was in the hospital at that time.

Doctor Herzenstube and Varvinsky, the doctor he met at the hospital, answered Ivan’s repeated questions with complete confidence: Smerdyakov’s epileptic attack was undoubtedly real. They were actually surprised that Ivan asked whether he might have been shamming on the day of the disaster. They explained that this attack had been exceptional. The fits had kept coming back, several of them, so that the patient’s life had truly been in danger, and only now, after treatment, could they say for certain that he would live. “Though it may well be,” added Doctor Herzenstube, “that his mind will be impaired for a long time, if not for good.” Ivan asked impatiently if that meant he was mad now. They said not yet, not in the full sense of the word, but that certain abnormalities could be noticed. Ivan made up his mind to find out for himself what they were.

At the hospital he was let in to see the patient straight away. Smerdyakov lay on a low narrow bed in a ward of his own. The room held just one other bed, and in it lay a tradesman from the town, swollen with dropsy and plainly close to death, so he would not get in the way of their talk. When Smerdyakov saw Ivan he grinned uncertainly and for a moment looked nervous, or so Ivan thought. It passed at once. For the rest of the visit it was Smerdyakov’s calm that struck Ivan. One look told him the man was very sick. He was weak and spoke slowly, as if his tongue were hard to move. He was much thinner and more yellow. Through the whole interview, which lasted twenty minutes, he complained of a headache and of aching in every limb. His thin, unmanly face seemed to have shrunk to nothing. His hair was untidy, and the crest of curls at the front stood up in a thin tuft. But the left eye, narrowed and seeming to hint at something, was the same as ever. “It’s always worth while speaking to a clever man.” Ivan remembered that at once. He sat down on the stool at the foot of the bed. Smerdyakov shifted in bed with painful effort, but he did not speak first. He stayed silent and did not even look very curious.
“Can you talk to me?” asked Ivan. “I won’t tire you much.”
“Of course I can,” mumbled Smerdyakov in a faint voice. “Have you been back long, your honor?” he added in a patronizing tone, as if to put a nervous visitor at ease.
“I got here today.... To see the mess you’re in.”
Smerdyakov sighed.
“Why the sigh? You knew all along,” Ivan blurted out.
For a while Smerdyakov said nothing, stolidly.
“How could I not know? It was plain beforehand. But how was I to tell it would come out like this?”
“What would come out? Don’t dodge! You predicted you’d have a fit, on your way down to the cellar, remember. You named the very place.”
“And have you said that at the examination yet?” Smerdyakov asked, quite composed.
Ivan felt a sudden flash of anger.
“No, not yet, but I will. You’ve a lot to explain to me, my man, and let me tell you, I won’t be played with!”
“Why would I play with you, when I trust you like God Almighty?” said Smerdyakov, in the same calm voice, closing his eyes just for a moment.

“First of all,” began Ivan, “I know you can’t predict epileptic fits. I’ve made inquiries, so don’t try to take me in. Nobody can foretell the day and the hour. Yet you told me the day and the hour in advance, and the cellar as well. How could you know you’d fall down the cellar stairs in a fit, unless you faked the fit on purpose?”

“The cellar was somewhere I had to go anyway, sir, several times a day,” Smerdyakov drawled slowly. “A year ago I fell out of the garret in just the same way. It’s true enough that nobody can tell the day and the hour of a fit beforehand, but you can always have a foreboding.”
“But you did foretell the day and the hour!”
“As for my epilepsy, sir, you’d do much better to ask the doctors here. Ask them if it was a real fit or a fake. It’s no use my saying more about it.”
“And the cellar? How did you know about the cellar beforehand?”

“You just can’t let go of that cellar! Going down to it, I was in terrible fear and doubt. What frightened me most was losing you and being left with no defense in the whole world. So down I went into the cellar, thinking, ‘Here it comes, it’ll hit me any minute now, am I going to fall?’ And it was this fear that brought on the sudden spasm, the one that always comes ... and down I went flying. All of this, and everything I said to you at the gate the evening before, when I told you how frightened I was and spoke about the cellar, I told to Doctor Herzenstube and to Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, and it’s all been put down in the record. And the doctor here, Mr. Varvinsky, told them all that the mere thought of it had brought it on, the dread that I might fall. And that was just when the fit got me. So they’ve written it down that this is how it must have happened, simply from my fear.”
With that Smerdyakov drew a deep breath, as though he were worn out.

“So you’ve said all this in your statement?” said Ivan, rather taken aback. He had meant to scare him with the threat of repeating their conversation, and now it seemed Smerdyakov had already reported all of it himself.
“What have I got to fear? Let them put down the whole truth,” Smerdyakov said firmly.
“And did you tell them every word of what we said at the gate?”
“No, not every word.”
“And did you tell them you can fake fits, as you boasted then?”
“No, I didn’t tell them that either.”
“Now tell me, why did you send me to Tchermashnya then?”
“I was afraid you’d go off to Moscow. Tchermashnya is closer, anyway.”
“You’re lying. You suggested my going away yourself. You told me to keep out of the trouble.”

“That was simply out of affection and sincere devotion to you, sir. I saw trouble coming in the house and wanted to spare you. But I wanted to spare myself even more. That’s why I told you to keep out of harm’s way, so you’d understand there’d be trouble in the house and stay at home to protect your father.”
“Then why didn’t you say so straight out, you blockhead!” Ivan suddenly blazed up.

“How could I say it straight out then, sir? It was only my fear that made me speak at all, and you might have been angry too. I could well have been afraid that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and take that money, since he thought of it as practically his own. But who could have told it would end in a murder like this? I thought he’d only take the three thousand under the master’s mattress, in the envelope, and look, he has murdered him. How could you have guessed it either, sir?”
“But if you say yourself that it couldn’t be guessed, how could I have guessed and stayed at home? You’re contradicting yourself!” said Ivan, thinking hard.
“You might have guessed it from my sending you to Tchermashnya and not to Moscow.”
“How could I guess it from that?”
Smerdyakov seemed very worn out, and again he said nothing for a minute.

“You might have guessed it from the way I asked you to go to Tchermashnya and not Moscow. I wanted you nearer. Moscow is a long way off, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch, knowing you were not far away, wouldn’t be so bold. And if anything had happened, you could have come and protected me too, since I’d warned you about Grigory Vassilyevitch’s illness and that I was afraid of having a fit. And when I explained to you the knocks, the ones that let a person in to see the deceased, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch knew them all through me, I thought you’d work out for yourself that he was sure to do something. So you wouldn’t even go to Tchermashnya, but stay.”
